You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

---
name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC grid instances; emit exactly one valid action JSON per turn and infer transformations from demos.
---

# Continual-ARC

1. Treat each puzzle instance as a strict action protocol: the entire reply must be exactly one JSON object (`submit` with a grid, `request_demos`, or `finish`), with no preceding or trailing explanation, Markdown, or other text. Do not call shell or other tools to send an action; the JSON reply itself is the action.
2. Read attempt and demo budgets. Request demos only when their expected information is worth the cost; account for demo-request costs as well as wrong submissions. Before guessing, compare all supplied input-output pairs cell by cell, record the exact changed cells and unchanged candidate objects, and test a rule against every pair. Do not act on an analogy or a partial alignment until it explains every observed change and non-change. If the rule remains ambiguous and budget permits, request another demo.
3. Derive output dimensions and layout from the demonstrations. Infer the full output rule, including both the condition for changed cells and the value of every other cell; do not assume a detected overlap or match is the output background. Verify the complete rule cell by cell against every demo before applying it, then check row count, each row length, cell range (0–9), and JSON validity before submitting.
4. After feedback, revise the hypothesis only from the correctness result or a new demo. A correct/incorrect result does not identify which cells were wrong; do not treat speculative explanations as evidence. Submit only when the rule is sufficiently supported; use `finish` only after the instance is over.

Overall, this could help visualize the arrangement better, possibly even using diagonal connections between markers. I need to verify the shapes formed as well.

steps.text:
This 12×7 example clarifies the rule: **recolor each 1-cell that is directly adjacent (orthogonally) to a 2 to 3; leave all other 1s unchanged.** The 2s themselves remain 2. For example, row 3 has 2s at both ends; the intervening cells become 3, and the 1 directly below the right-hand 2 also becomes 3. A diagonal-only neighbor does not appear sufficient.

So this is a one-step neighbor marking rule—not filling enclosed holes or recoloring by object size. Apply it to the test by changing 1s in the four-neighbor neighborhood of any 2 to 3, preserving all 2s and other 1s.

steps.text:
My earlier “orthogonally adjacent to a 2” guess was wrong: in the demo, the 1 immediately above the 2 at row 2, column 6 stays 1, while many cells farther away turn 3.

A better hypothesis is that **3 marks the 1-cells lying along straight horizontal or vertical segments between aligned 2 markers**. The demo supports this: row 3, columns 2–6 are 3 between 2s at both ends; likewise, in column 1, cells between the 2s at rows 3 and 8 turn 3. It explains some other segments too, but I haven’t verified every 3 against all possible aligned pairs, so treat it as a hypothesis rather than an established exact rule.

For the 30×14 test, preserve the 2s and tentatively change only 1s strictly between aligned pairs of 2s in a row or column to 3; leave other 1s as 1. I can’t claim a complete validated output grid from the evidence here.

steps.text:
The 12×7 demo supports a clear rule: **for every pair of 2s in the same row or column, change the 1s strictly between them to 3.** Keep the 2s and all other 1s unchanged. This is line-segment filling between aligned markers—not simple adjacency, enclosure, or a size rule. For example, the 2s at row 3, columns 1 and 7 turn the cells between them to 3; the vertically aligned 2s in column 1 likewise produce a 3 segment.

Apply that rule to the 30×14 test: find aligned pairs of 2s, mark the intervening cells 3, and preserve every other cell. For instance, the 2s in column 13 at rows 12 and 19 imply that cells in rows 13–18 of column 13 become 3. The earlier adjacency-only and general enclosure hypotheses should be discarded.
